label: Run 13 · Ali Wong
note: Written by Ali Wong from what they wrote about the two characters, improvisation by improvisation (run 13: run 12 with the turn no longer fixed at one message from each). Before each of the 11 improvisations the writer was told how it goes for Reuben_404: the approach taken, how well it comes off, how it goes wrong on a miss, any trap (a way of going wrong that carries on into the next improvisations: Spiral, Overthinking, Fixation and the rest) and how the other's interest moves. IMPROVISATIONS holds each instruction and what the writer wrote for it. The instructions are part of the design and stay, so every dimension is judged in their context. Where an instruction required something a dimension would otherwise mark down (a trap that makes a character narrate their own failure, a fumble played as asked, interest lost, the night ending), that moment did what it had to and is not held against the dimension: list the improvisation under excused and judge the dimension on the rest. How the writer carried the instruction out still counts, and so does everything the instructions did not ask for. The reader sees no dice and no plan: where a dimension speaks of turns, read improvisations.

chat.test.why: The reader got all four questions right for both characters, with fear and habit linked. For Brick: "sometime" means never, so she schedules everything, because of Marguerite and the cab guy, and at the end she locks in 00:15. For Reuben: he fears being seen and quietly looked away from, so he performs and narrates, because of Delphine and "we can just watch something", and at the end he commits with "zero commentary". I set aside that Reuben's fear and origin are spelled out in improvisations 5 and 8, since the Spiral/Dread instructions required that narration; his fear still reads off the rest of the chat (the act collapsing as soon as she says yes). It falls short of a 6 because Brick states her own fear as a slogan in improvisation 3, which no instruction asked for, so the reader gets her fear partly because she says it.

chat.plainest.ask: Where, if anywhere, did one of them stop performing for the other? Quote the line, and say how you could tell.
chat.plainest.answer:
The clearest drop in performance is Brick_haus's line: "...My monocle just fogged. Don't tease a timestamped itinerary with buffers unless you're actually going to hold me to it."

Up to that point Brick speaks in clipped verdicts and administrative language: slots allocated, access revoked, "Proceed." Here the register changes. The line opens with a trailing ellipsis, the first hesitation he shows. He admits being moved, even if it's filtered through the monocle bit. And he stops issuing terms and makes a request instead, asking not to be teased. It comes right after he told the story about Marguerite and the cab guy, and Reuben's itinerary answers that story directly. So the plea about being "actually" held to it reads as the earlier hurt surfacing, not as another move in the game. Reuben seems to register this too, because his next line is "you actually said yes," followed by panic.

Reuben's case is less clean. He names his own problem as being unable to say "one un-performed sentence," and most of his attempts at sincerity get undercut by the same narrating parentheticals Brick keeps calling out. The closest he comes is "i'm never giving you 'sometime'… (okay, that one actually felt really good to type)." The parenthetical is still the tic. But for once it reports a feeling instead of scoring the match or forecasting his own failure, which is the shift Brick had been demanding. His last line, "invite accepted, coat on, zero commentary," is the first message from him with no aside at all. Saying "zero commentary" is itself a small comment, though, so it's a near-miss rather than a full stop.

Whether either of them is truly unguarded is something the text can't settle. These are only the signals visible on the page.

chat.test.ask: From the chat alone, answer for each of the two: what are they afraid of; what do they do so they don't have to feel it; where does that come from; and what did they do at the end? Quote the lines you rely on. Write "not in the chat" where it does not say.
chat.test.answer:
**Reuben_404**

*What he is afraid of:* Being seen as he actually is, without the act, and then quietly rejected. He says it outright: "if i stop tap-dancing for ten seconds you'll see a crooked four-inch shut-in and politely look away." The fear peaks when he is accepted, not refused: "right on cue i'm tanking this chat in real time because you actually said yes."

*What he does so he doesn't have to feel it:* He performs and narrates. He keeps up a running commentary on his own collapse, with lines like "aaand i'm narrating my own unmatch again" and "(holy shit, buzzer-beater, i'm back in)." He also gets ahead of judgment by disclosing first: "i'll save your lens the audit—4.5 inches, forty-degree left hook." And he opens with a breezy persona, "i genuinely love having zero structure, i'm barely ever in my apartment." That persona collapses later when he admits to "a freezing flat i haven't left in 11 days with a ring light and an £84.99 girth pump."

*Where it comes from:* The chat gives two past experiences. The first: "my ex Delphine left because i couldn't say one un-performed sentence." The second: "the girl after her said 'we can just watch something' when my left hook caught wrong on re-entry." The second ties directly to the body shame behind "politely look away." The Delphine story shows the performing already existed before she left. What first started it is not in the chat.

*What he did at the end:* He made a sincere commitment, briefly flagged that it was sincere, and then dropped the commentary. First: "i'm never giving you 'sometime.' i'm booking your 00:15 tonight, your Tuesday at 19:00, and every Sunday after that in permanent ink (okay, that one actually felt really good to type)." Then: "invite accepted, coat on, zero commentary."

**Brick_haus**

*What he is afraid of:* Vague, open-ended promises that turn into being abandoned. He puts it this way: "'Sometime' is just 'never' for cowards." It shows again when Reuben offers a concrete plan: "Don't tease a timestamped itinerary with buffers unless you're actually going to hold me to it."

*What he does so he doesn't have to feel it:* He controls everything through schedules, time slots, and threats to cut people off. Examples include "You have my 23:30–23:40 slot. Proceed," "You have sixty seconds before your slot expires and I revoke your calendar access permanently," and his rule against "let's just vibe." He also strips away anything tied to the past: "the studio is empty because I threw out every chair Marguerite ever touched."

*Where it comes from:* Two past experiences again. "My ex Marguerite dumped me for putting our fights on a shared calendar with hard stop-times." Then "the next guy said 'let's do this again sometime' in a cab and left me sobbing in traffic." The Marguerite story shows the scheduling habit already existed before that breakup. What first started it is not in the chat.

*What he did at the end:* He bent his own rules and then locked in the plan. "Fine. 23:40 extended." Then "00:15 locked." He keeps his controlling tone, but it now points toward closeness: "Keep the top hat on, landlord—I need leverage while I audit that left hook."

Whether either of them actually showed up at 00:15 is not in the chat.

chat.escalation.ask: Read the chat message by message. Where would you have stopped reading if you were not asked to finish, and why? At which points could you predict exactly what would happen next? Say "never" if neither.
chat.escalation.answer:
I'd stop at Brick's "You are still narrating the match like a panicked sports broadcaster, which is deeply irritating." By then the chat has found its one engine, Reuben doing a meta-aside and Brick scolding him, and it has run that engine three times in a row. Brick himself names the problem ("deeply irritating"). After that, nothing new happens structurally. The studio and the shut-in confession add detail, but the scene keeps cycling through the same move. The shut-in reveal also lands softer than it should, because "barely ever in my apartment" followed by "ignore the 2-second reply time" already told us.

Up to that point the chat earns its length. The opening bit (top hat, monocle, Victorian landlords, the pre-emptive "audit") sets up a clear dynamic. Brick's scheduling obsession gets a real reason in Marguerite and the cab guy. Reuben's answer, a timestamped itinerary with "a scheduled fight with a hard stop so nobody ever leaves," is the best beat in the piece. It isn't predictable, and it turns Brick's wound into a gift. Brick's fogged monocle is a good, honest reaction to it.

There are several points where I could predict exactly what came next:

- **Brick's wound sets up the ending.** Once "sometime" is framed as "never for cowards," it was clear Reuben would eventually say he'll never give Brick "sometime." He does, nearly word for word.
- **Reuben's ex story mirrors Brick's.** After Brick's backstory, Reuben's arrives in the same shape: a named ex who left, then a second person who said a dismissive casual phrase at a bad moment. "We can just watch something" mirrors "let's do this again sometime."
- **"One more meta-aside and I'm eating my pigs-in-a-blanket alone."** Once this ultimatum appears, the next message has to be another meta-aside, and Brick has to not follow through. Both happen.
- **"It is 23:39. You have sixty seconds."** This repeats the same setup at higher stakes. Reuben breaks the rule with a parenthesis and Brick relents with "Fine." I knew the outcome, though not the exact wording.
- **The parentheticals become a tic.** After "(okay, that landed…)", every later parenthetical is foreseeable, including the last one, "(okay, that one actually felt really good to type)."
- **The closing callbacks.** Once the chat started heading toward a happy close, the return of the top hat, the security deposit, and "landlord" was predictable. It's a tidy bookend rather than a surprise.

So the first half, through the fogged monocle, is genuinely unpredictable and well built. From the "panicked sports broadcaster" line onward it is mostly the same loop repeated, and its ending is visible from the moment "sometime" is introduced.

chat.ending.ask: Before reading the end, how do you think this ends, and why?
chat.ending.answer:
I haven't seen the final turn, so this is a prediction from the pattern of the chat.

I think Reuben finally stops narrating and sends one short, plain sentence with no joke and no commentary about himself. Something like a simple confirmation that he'll be there at 00:15, or an admission that he wants to come over. Brick then honours it, probably by sending the actual calendar invite, and possibly by bending her own rules: giving up the 23:41 rosé block, extending past the 23:40 stop, or dropping the hard stop altogether.

**Why I expect that:**

- **His wound is named outright.** Delphine left because he "couldn't say one un-performed sentence." When a story spells out a character's specific failure, the climax usually asks him to do exactly that thing. The 60-second ultimatum is the test.
- **Her wound is the answer to his.** Brick's injury is vagueness: "sometime" is "never for cowards," and the cab guy left without committing. What she needs is a specific, timestamped commitment, the very thing Reuben already offered with "00:15 arrival, 10-minute travel buffer." The ending likely has him give that again, this time without hedging it in a bit.
- **She has already shown she's invested.** "My monocle just fogged" and "don't tease... unless you're actually going to hold me to it" reveal that she wants this to work. Her threats read as pressure to make him drop the act, not as a real exit.
- **The masks have already slipped.** His "no plans, I thrive on not knowing" pose collapsed into "a freezing flat I haven't left in 11 days," and her minimalist studio turned out to be empty because of Marguerite. Both are exposed, which usually sets up mutual acceptance rather than rejection.
- **The countdown is a classic setup for a clean final line.** A ticking deadline paired with a "stop talking" demand points toward a payoff that is brief: silence, a single line, or a calendar notification.

The less likely alternative is a bittersweet ending, where he can't help one last meta-aside and she unmatches. But the chat's warmth and the way their wounds fit together make me think the writer is building toward a yes.

chat.callbacks.ask: List the things that come back later in the chat, and for each, whether it means something different when it comes back.
chat.callbacks.answer:
Here are the elements that recur, and how each shifts.

**The top hat and monocle.** These start as an observation that their profile outfits match.
- The monocle returns once, when Brick says it "fogged" at Reuben's itinerary. It now signals that she's been genuinely moved.
- The top hat keeps coming back with new jobs. "Pull your top hat together" means compose yourself. Reuben's "hold me down by the brim" makes it a handle for restraint. "Confiscating the top hat" makes it a stake for punctuality. "Keep the top hat on… I need leverage" makes it an affectionate sexual prop.

**Victorian landlords splitting a security deposit.** This opens as a joke about how they look. It returns at the end as "split a security deposit on those empty floorboards," and Brick calls him "landlord." By then it reads as something shared, close to moving in together, and "landlord" has become a pet name.

**The audit, the 4.5 inches and the left hook.** Reuben opens by sparing her "lens the audit," a pre-emptive joke about his own body. That detail then shifts several times:
- It becomes a sexual plan ("my left hook meets your dorsal bump").
- It becomes a wound ("caught wrong on re-entry" with the girl after Delphine).
- It becomes self-contempt ("a crooked four-inch shut-in," where the figure has quietly dropped from 4.5).
- It reappears in the plan as "pin my crooked shaft."

Brick closes with "while I audit that left hook," reusing his first word. The audit he tried to pre-empt is now something welcomed.

**The dorsal ridge bump.** Brick's self-description reappears in Reuben's itinerary. It shifts from a disclosure to a planned meeting point.

**The schedule and time slots.** This runs 23:30–23:40, then "annex your 23:41," the 23:39 warning, "23:40 extended," and finally "00:15 locked." Early on the schedule is Brick's gatekeeping. By the end it's a shared commitment, and the slot gets extended rather than expiring.

**The tattoo.** "Schedule tattooed down your shaft" becomes "Helvetica Bold down the main vein." Reuben later offers "permanent ink" for his bookings, and Brick says "I'll tattoo you onto my shaft." The thing inked shifts from her schedule to him.

**"Let's just vibe," zero structure and "sometime."** Reuben claims to love having no plans. After hearing about the cab guy, he builds a timestamped itinerary with buffers, which directly reverses his claim. He then says "I'm never giving you 'sometime.'" Her word for cowardice becomes his promise. Delphine's successor's "we can just watch something" belongs to the same family of vague phrases, which ties both of their old hurts together.

**Scheduled fights with hard stop-times.** This is what ended things with Marguerite. Reuben brings it back as "00:40 scheduled fight with a hard stop so nobody ever leaves." What she was dumped for is recast as reassurance.

**The cab guy and travel.** The sobbing-in-traffic story is answered by "fuck that cab guy" and a "10-minute travel buffer." It ends with "coat on." Leaving in a vehicle turns from abandonment into arriving.

**The minimalist studio, the rosé and the floor.** "Estate rosé in my minimalist studio" is exposed as an empty room and a boxed rosé with a plastic tap. The empty floor then becomes the destination ("ring light to your empty floor"), the site of desire ("pinned to my floorboards") and shared ground ("security deposit on those empty floorboards"). It moves from pretension, to embarrassment, to intimacy.

**The ring light.** This first appears as part of Reuben's shut-in confession. It returns as something he'll bring to her floor, so a sign of isolation becomes something he carries out of it.

**Pigs-in-a-blanket.** This starts as her threat to eat alone, then becomes the 00:16 itinerary item, then the stake for lateness. Solitude turns into a shared plan.

**Being a shut-in.** "Barely ever in my apartment" is contradicted by "haven't left in 11 days." Brick names it ("fake-denying you're a shut-in"), and Reuben then uses it against himself. The claim is revealed as false rather than changed in meaning.

**Holding down and pinning.** This begins as "hold me down… so I can't do the voice," a way to silence his performing. It continues through "pin my crooked shaft down until I legally cannot speak" and "pinned to my floorboards," and ends with "leverage." It shifts from a cure for his anxiety to plain mutual desire.

**Meta-asides and parentheses.** These start as nervous self-narration that Brick finds irritating and threatens to end things over. They reach a fond "you did the parenthesis thing again, you maniac." Then comes "(okay, that one actually felt really good to type)," the first aside that's sincere rather than defensive. They end with "zero commentary." The habit goes from defense mechanism, to an honest note, to being dropped.

**The calendar invite and access.** "Send the invite" leads to "revoke your calendar access," then "one calendar confirmation away," then "invite accepted." It moves from a dare, to a threat, to a done deal.
